title: Eight-bit sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement
summary: Compare how positive and negative integers convert across the three encodings, and see why two's complement has only one representation of zero.
description: The figure arranges sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement in three rows comparing +0, +5, −0, and −28, each written as 8 bits grouped into two 4-bit nibbles. Bidirectional arrows connect sign-magnitude with one's complement and one's complement with two's complement; the notes on the right state the forward rules for converting a negative number from sign-magnitude to one's complement and then to two's complement.

frames.title: Eight-bit sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement
frames.explanation: The highest bit is the sign bit, and +0 and +5 have identical bit patterns across all three representations. For a negative number, keep the leading sign bit 1 and invert only the lower 7 bits to get the one's complement, then add 1 and keep the lower 8 bits to get the two's complement. In the table, −28 follows this rule; the reverse conversion subtracts 1 from the two's complement and then inverts the lower 7 bits while keeping the sign bit to return to sign-magnitude. Adding 1 to the one's complement of −0 (1111 1111) produces the nine-bit value 1 0000 0000; discarding the carry-out leaves 0000 0000, identical to +0, so positive zero and negative zero can no longer be distinguished from the two's complement.
